# Evidence Base and Research Needs {#sec-evidence-needs}

Grassland birds are more abundant on planted solar sites than on the farmland around them, and that is known because people went out and counted them [@walston2025]. The claim that a seeded ground layer under an array keeps sediment and nitrogen out of the creek below is a different kind of claim. It is the prairie-strip result from corn and soybean fields [@schulte2017], carried over onto ground nobody has sampled. Both claims appear in this lexicon, and the sentences that make them look alike.

Every judgment this lexicon makes about how well something is known lives in this chapter. The other chapters describe what [agrisolar](terminology.qmd#term-agrisolar) design is and what it can do. This one says what is established, what is inferred, and what nobody has measured. Keeping it all in one place lets a reader weigh the whole lexicon at once, and keeps any chapter from quietly overstating its own confidence.

It is organized by what would fix each gap rather than by topic. Some gaps need a season of field instruments, some need somebody to go back to the original data, and some need a project that does not exist yet to be built and reported.

## What the evidence supports {#sec-eb-status}

Read this as the confidence behind each chapter, stated once here rather than repeated as a caveat wherever a claim appears.

**Water** (§-@sec-fn-hydrologic). The link between shade and soil moisture in dry places is **verified** [@barrongafford2019; @sturchio2025; @pinos2026], though limited at some sites [@kannenberg2023]. Evidence on infiltration and recharge at depth is still **thin** [@yavari2022]. Interception is documented for prairie strips in cropland [@schulte2017], but never yet from beneath an array. Avoided loading is **arithmetic rather than measurement**: it follows from fertilizer application rates on retired acreage, not from a monitored stream.

**Ecology** (§-@sec-fn-biodiversity). **Verified** for gains in grassland birds [@walston2025], the response of insect communities [@walston2024], and bee diversity in arrays planted for pollinators [@bruningasocolar2025]. Scorecards write the choices down, though what each one gives credit for differs [@epri2021]. The gain **depends on context**. It is largest where the surrounding landscape has little natural habitat left, so its size depends on what the site would otherwise have been, not on the planting alone.

**Agriculture and soils** (§-@sec-fn-agricultural). On the farming side, pollinators moving into nearby crops is **verified** [@walston2024], and the farmland within foraging distance has been mapped [@walston2018]. Pest control is **inferred, not measured** at solar sites, and a change in yield or input costs that can be pinned on an array is **not established anywhere**. On the soil side, early gains are **verified** for [ecovoltaic](terminology.qmd#term-ecovoltaics) grassland restoration [@krasner2025], and long-run build-up is thinly measured [@carvalho2024]. The size of the construction debt is the least measured part of the soil account, and among the most likely to decide whether the soil comes out ahead or behind, because the reported gains come from sites whose earthworks are not described.

**Communities and economy** (§-@sec-fn-community). The design principle is **verified** in the ecovoltaic frameworks themselves, where @tolgyesi2023 make a workable business model, with stakeholder involvement built in, one of five equal pillars. The costs to communities are better measured than the benefits [@bessette2024; @elmallah2023]. Which arrangements deliver lasting, fairly shared benefit is still thinly evidenced.

**The community scale, A3** (§-@sec-community-scale). Thin, and thinner than the confidence with which the middle sizes are usually discussed. The capacity arithmetic is solid and comes from federal sources. How pollination benefits travel is measured, at two sites, for one function. Everything else is inference. Nobody has compared several small arrays against one large one at the same capacity and management. Nobody has tested whether land quality varies with project size at a finer scale than the whole parcel. And nobody has evaluated whether the bonuses that state incentive programs pay for farming or pollinator habitat changed what actually got built. The [outcomes footprint](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale) is under-evidenced at every zone on the transect, not only here. The A3 section argues about where the decision still lies. It does not report where restoration has already happened.

**The regional calibration** (§-@sec-regionality). The numbers in that section are *trace before citing*: they come from secondary and program sources and have not been checked against the original records. The regional argument does not depend on any one of them.

**What the siting studies show.** @wu2026siting studies [utility-scale](terminology.qmd#term-utility-scale) projects of 1 MW and up, treating each project as a single data point. It does not test whether the factors driving site choice change with project size. So it shows what large projects are sited around, but not the contrast with smaller projects that the lexicon draws. That contrast still rests on @macknick2022, @boggis2020, and the archetypes, which is weaker evidence than a study broken out by size would be. That is why where [siting latitude](terminology.qmd#term-siting-latitude) peaks is still an open question. @owusuobeng2025 is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

**The prime-farmland argument.** Studies that score solar sites by soil quality find that distribution-scale projects sit disproportionately on good land, and it is tempting to read that as careless siting. Two things complicate that reading.

The first is a hidden third factor. Community-scale solar goes where the electricity is used, electricity is used where people live, and people live where the good soil was, because towns grew up on good farmland. That is why metropolitan areas hold an outsized share of the nation's [prime farmland](terminology.qmd#term-prime-farmland), and why development has pressed on the best soils for a century [@dillman1982]. A fleet built near where power is used will sit on prime soil whether or not anyone was careless.

The second is the level of detail. A parcel classed as prime farmland is not equally productive everywhere. Across 338 Midwest fields and 1,625 yield maps, about half of the field area yielded well year after year, **32% was persistently low-yielding**, and 18% swung with the weather, with the unstable ground concentrated in wet low spots [@maestrini2018]. Roughly a third of a prime field never performs. That 32% is exactly what the freedom to choose a site at A3 can act on. A study that scores a site by the soil class of its whole parcel cannot see whether the array took the good part or the bad part. So the claim that mid-sized projects are sited carelessly and the claim that they are sited well are both, for now, untested at the level of detail that would settle them.

## Measurements nobody has made yet {#sec-rn-measurements}

| Gap | Flagged at | What would close it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Nutrient and sediment interception under an array.** Whether a seeded solar ground layer performs like a prairie strip. | §-@sec-fn-hydrologic | Paired monitoring above and below an array sited on a flow path, against a strip or an unplanted control. |
| **Recharge and the water balance at depth.** Panel drip, altered cover, and what reaches the aquifer. | §-@sec-fn-hydrologic | Measured drip and runoff, soil-moisture profiles, and coupled surface–groundwater modeling on instrumented sites. |
| **Cumulative effect on one watershed.** Whether arrays scattered through the same watershed add up, cancel out, or miss each other, and how much of the ground has to drain through them before a gauge can tell. | §-@sec-fn-hydrologic | Gauged watersheds filling up with solar, against comparable ones without, and routing models built on those rather than one site at a time. |
| **Soil carbon over decades.** Early gains are measured; the multi-decade curve is not. | §-@sec-fn-agricultural | Re-sampling the early [ecovoltaic](terminology.qmd#term-ecovoltaics) sites on a decadal schedule, which needs a commitment longer than a grant cycle. |
| **The construction debt, and how long it takes to repay.** How much carbon mass grading costs a site, against how much a minimally graded build keeps. | §-@sec-fn-agricultural | Paired sampling before and after construction across projects with contrasting earthworks, which needs the earthworks recorded at the time. |
| **Pest regulation from an array.** Natural-enemy habitat is established for perennial refuge, never demonstrated from a solar site. | §-@sec-fn-agricultural | Natural-enemy and pest counts in fields at increasing distance from a planted array. |
| **A yield or input-cost change attributable to the array.** The step a farmer actually cares about. | §-@sec-fn-agricultural | Paired fields near and far from a planted array, with pollination and pest pressure measured alongside yield. |
| **Whether a regional fleet of arrays functions as a connected network.** Compatible seed mixes and calendars make one on paper; nothing establishes that dispersal actually happens between sites. | §-@sec-fn-biodiversity | Mark–recapture or genetic work on a taxon whose dispersal distance is known, across arrays at a range of separations, with unbuilt patches as controls. |
| **Whether co-located ground supports biodiversity the way unbuilt ground does.** | §-@sec-fn-biodiversity, and the stated gap in @brock2026 | Comparative survey across co-located, conventional, and unbuilt sites in the same landscape. |
| **Which benefit structures deliver durable, fairly shared benefit.** The instruments are known; their outcomes are not. | §-@sec-fn-community | Longitudinal work on host communities rather than one-time acceptance surveys, with landowner and tenant reported separately. |

: The measurements that would settle claims this lexicon has to make on inference. Each is flagged where the chapters raise it, so a reader can check the claim rather than take the priority on faith. {#tbl-measurement-gaps}

The first of these has the most riding on it. Interception is the water-quality approach most projects could actually use, since it asks only for a seed mix and a placement rather than for retiring a working field. Right now it is supported entirely by analogy.

## Numbers that circulate without a traceable source {#sec-rn-tracing}

Some of this work is reading rather than measurement. The [Sources](sources.qmd) chapter splits what has been checked from what has not, and the unverified block is not a list of doubts so much as a list of errands.

::: {.caution}
**The grazing-cost figures are actively misquoted.** @stewart2025 report @mccall2023's $279/ha/yr as the median cost of sheep grazing. In McCall's Table 4, that figure is actually the median *mowing* cost at sheep-grazed sites, and grazing itself ran about $50/acre/yr (§-@sec-zones). Both readings are now in circulation, and converting between acres and hectares makes the confusion worse. Anyone quoting a grazing cost should go straight to McCall's table, and anyone who has already quoted the swapped figure should check which one they used.
:::

The regional figures in §-@sec-regionality are the largest block of untraced material: sunlight ranges, grid-queue and [curtailment](terminology.qmd#term-tracking-curtailment) sizes, community-solar capacities, [ground-coverage](terminology.qmd#term-gcr) thresholds, and the acreages under SGMA and over the Ogallala. The argument in that section does not depend on any single one of them, which is why they were kept. But none should appear in a permit filing or a paper until it has been traced. The [community-benefit](terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) and grazing-economics material sits in gray literature for a similar reason: it is real and widely practiced, but not yet pulled together anywhere citable.

## Claims that a counterexample would test {#sec-rn-counterexamples}

The lexicon makes several claims that could be wrong, and it is more useful if it names what would prove them wrong.

- **Sparing does not assemble at scale.** §-@sec-wedge holds that S4 thins toward A5 because idle remnants are scattered. A utility-scale project assembled from scattered [marginal](terminology.qmd#term-marginal-land) remnants on ordinary farmland, rather than from uniformly pre-disturbed ground, would reopen that corner. None is documented here, and one would be worth reporting.
- **Both hand-offs fall at A3.** @fig-siting-latitude puts the crossing from structure to management and the crossing from ownership to contracts in the same zone, and that is the main support for treating A3 as the zone with the most design freedom. Whether the peak sits at A2 or A3 is argued from the archetypes rather than measured, and the lines are schematic, not data. Moving the peak one zone to the left would move two claims, not one, so real siting decisions that put either crossing somewhere else would be worth reporting.
- **Regions resolve the pressures differently.** The [calibration](terminology.qmd#term-regional-calibration) in §-@sec-rg-us is a set of hypotheses. A region doing something its profile says it should not is the most useful single contribution the chapter can receive.
- **The six levers are complete and non-overlapping.** Every decision a project makes should land in exactly one of scale, siting, structure, management, ownership, and contracts. A decision that lands in none of them would mean the list is short; one that lands in all six would mean the categories are not cutting anything. The edge is the known partial exception, split deliberately between structure and management because a berm and a hedgerow fail differently (§-@sec-lv-physical).
- **The A3 ceiling rests on one untested number.** The zone tops out near 5 MW because a [restorative](terminology.qmd#term-restorative) community-scale array is taken to occupy at most about a third of its parcel (§-@sec-community-scale). More rests on that fraction than on any other number in the scheme, and it has not been tested against built projects. At half a parcel, the same fields would hold 3 to 7 MW, and the case for a higher ceiling partly comes back. Measuring how much of its parcel each of a set of built restorative community-scale arrays actually occupies would settle it.
- **The vocabulary describes a site, and sparing is a claim about a landscape.** Nothing here says where the array went instead. Statewide planning shows the gap matters. Siting New York's 2050 solar build to protect farmland spares roughly 80% of the farmland a least-cost build would take, but opens up more than 41,000 hectares of forest in the process [@gallaher2026]. Global models have the opposite problem. @brock2026 assign each map cell to a single land use and say plainly that they could not represent [co-location](terminology.qmd#term-colocation-integration), so their land-demand figures are upper limits and the arrangements this lexicon describes are invisible to them. Accounting at the landscape level that could handle both would test whether the axis needs a companion term.
- **Positions are exclusive.** The two-question reading rule (§-@sec-positions) should place any real project in exactly one position. A project that genuinely will not fit is a flaw in the axis, not in the project.

## What would make the evidence easier to build {#sec-rn-reporting}

These are recommendations about reporting, not about design. The lexicon prescribes an aim and leaves the dimensions to the site, and none of what follows is a dimension.

::: {.how-to}
1. **Report acreage alongside capacity.** Megawatts are how a project is filed; acres are how the ground experiences it, and the two come apart with tracking and [clearance](terminology.qmd#term-clearance) (§-@sec-zones).
2. **Name the [benefit delivery](terminology.qmd#term-benefit-delivery) when claiming a function.** A hydrologic claim that does not say whether it means moisture under the panels or nitrogen kept out of a creek cannot be checked, and the two need different evidence (§-@sec-benefit-range).
3. **Separate the landowner from the tenant.** Nearly 40% of Central Valley agricultural land is leased, and a conversion that sustains an owner can end the operation of the person farming the ground. Aggregate farm-income figures hide exactly the party most at risk (§-@sec-fn-community).
4. **Publish the counterfactual behind a sparing claim.** Sparing is a claim about land that was not taken, so it is only checkable against the local market and the sites genuinely in play (§-@sec-positions).
5. **State the prior land cover and the earthworks when reporting soil carbon.** Putting perennial cover on ground that was tilled and converting existing grassland are opposite transactions, and whether soil carbon goes up or down depends on which one happened. How much the site was graded belongs in the report too, because a gain measured on ground that was never stripped and a gain measured on ground rebuilding from a stockpile are not the same number (§-@sec-fn-agricultural).
6. **Give the region and the crop when reporting a shade-yield result.** Whether shade helps or hurts flips with air temperature, so a yield figure with no location attached travels farther than the evidence behind it (§-@sec-rg-factors).
7. **Report what did not work.** Establishment failures, seed mixes that did not take, and grazing arrangements that fell apart are absent from the literature and present on the ground, and their absence is why cost expectations are unreliable (§-@sec-zones).
:::
